title: Iuppiter et Venus. Fata Romae
titleEn: Jupiter Unrolls the Fates — Aeneid I.198–296
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: On the Libyan shore Aeneas, sick with worry, hides his fear and rallies his men with a short speech; they butcher the stags, roast them, drink, and talk anxiously of the friends still missing. Then the scene lifts to heaven. Venus, in tears, taxes Jupiter with the plain unfairness of the Trojans' lot: he promised them Rome, and yet Antenor, another Trojan, has long since settled safely in Italy. Jupiter smiles, kisses her, and answers with the poem's first great prophecy of Roman history: Aeneas's war and his city, Ascanius at Alba Longa, Romulus and Rome, empire without end, a Trojan Caesar, and an age of peace in which the gates of War are shut. Virgil's model for the opening speech is Odysseus' encouragement to his crew in Odyssey 12, and the scene in heaven, a god looking down on mortals, is a staple of Homeric epic, retold here for Rome.

sentences.t: “O socii—neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum—
sentences.l: “O comrades—for we are not ignorant, before this, of evils—
sentences.i: “Comrades—for hardship is nothing new to us—
sentences.n: Aeneas's speech to his men: a rallying speech to a crew after a disaster, rebuilt from Odysseus' address to his men before Scylla in Odyssey 12 (see the next lines). 'socii' — vocative, 'comrades' (allies, companions). 'ignari… malorum' — 'ignorant of evils': 'ignarus' takes the genitive. 'ante' is an adverb here, 'before, earlier'. The dashes mark the aside.

sentences.t: O passi graviora, dabit deus his quoque finem.
sentences.l: O you who have suffered heavier things, a god will give to these also an end.
sentences.i: You who have borne worse than this — a god will put an end to these troubles too.
sentences.n: 'O passi graviora' — 'passi' is the perfect participle of 'patior', vocative plural: 'O you having suffered'. 'graviora' is neuter plural comparative, 'heavier things', used as a noun. 'dabit deus' — 'a god will give': no particular god, just divine providence. 'his' — dative, 'to these (troubles)'. 'quoque' — 'also'.

sentences.t:
Vos et Scyllaeam rabiem penitusque sonantis
accestis scopulos, vos et Cyclopea saxa
experti:
sentences.l:
You both Scylla's fury and the deep-sounding
rocks approached, you also the Cyclopean stones
have tested:
sentences.i: You have faced Scylla's fury and the crags that boom from deep within; you have tried the Cyclops' boulders:
sentences.n: 'Vos et… vos et' — 'you both… you also': the repeated pronoun makes the two sets of dangers equal. 'Scyllaeam rabiem' — Scylla, the sea-monster with barking dogs round her waist, who snatches sailors from passing ships; the 'sounding rocks' are the cliffs of her cave, which boom with the sea. 'sonantis' — Greenough's -is for the accusative plural (you'll see this constantly: 'montis', 'omnis', 'iacentis'). 'accestis' = 'accessistis', a shortened perfect (compare '-ere' for '-erunt'). 'Cyclopea saxa' — the boulders hurled by Polyphemus in Odyssey 9. The whole speech echoes Odyssey 12, where Odysseus tells his crew they have escaped the Cyclops and will one day remember this too.

sentences.t:
revocate animos, maestumque timorem
mittite:
sentences.l:
call back your spirits, and gloomy fear
send away:
sentences.i: gather your spirits again and let this heavy dread go:
sentences.n: 'revocate animos' — 'call your spirits back', as if courage had gone off and must be summoned. 'maestum timorem' — 'sad, gloomy fear'; the adjective is transferred from the men's mood to the fear itself. 'mittite' — 'send away, let go'. Imperatives in short clauses: the style of a commander on the beach.

sentences.t: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit.
sentences.l: perhaps even these things, some day, it will please to remember.
sentences.i: Perhaps there will come a day when we are glad to call even this to mind.
sentences.n: The most quoted line of the poem, or very nearly. 'forsan' — 'perhaps' (a poetic word, with the verb in the indicative here). 'et haec' — 'even these things', neuter plural and the object of 'meminisse': the whole ordeal. 'meminisse' is the perfect infinitive of 'memini', which has present meaning ('to remember'); the infinitive is itself the subject of 'iuvabit' — literally 'to remember will please', 'it will be pleasing to remember'. 'olim' — 'some day', looking forward as well as back. Virgil's source is Odyssey 12, where Odysseus tells his men that he thinks they will remember these troubles too; Aeneas's version reaches further, past the voyage itself, to a time when it will be a pleasure to speak of it.

sentences.t:
Per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum
tendimus in Latium;
sentences.l:
Through various chances, through so many crises of affairs
we press on to Latium;
sentences.i: Through all these shifting fortunes, through so many perils, we hold our course for Latium;
sentences.n: 'per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum' — the repeated 'per' piles up the hardships; 'discrimina rerum' — 'crises of affairs' (a 'discrimen' is a point of decision and danger). 'tendimus in Latium' — we stretch, strain, make for; 'Latium' is the land around Rome, here named by Aeneas himself as the goal of the voyage.

sentences.t:
sedes ubi fata quietas
ostendunt;
sentences.l:
seats, where the fates peaceful
show;
sentences.i: where the fates reveal a place of rest;
sentences.n: 'sedes… quietas' — 'quiet, settled dwelling-places': 'sedes' is the home Aeneas has been promised (Apollo at Delos, in Book 3, speaks of an 'ancient mother' to be sought). 'ubi' is placed late in its clause. 'fata' — the fates, the sequence of what Jupiter has decreed, a word that will mean more and more as the poem goes on.

sentences.t: illic fas regna resurgere Troiae.
sentences.l: there it is lawful that the kingdoms rise again of Troy.
sentences.i: there Troy's kingdom is destined to rise again.
sentences.n: 'illic fas (est)' — 'there it is right, permitted by divine law': 'fas' is what the gods allow, as opposed to 'ius', human law. The verb 'est' is left out (you'll see this constantly). 'regna resurgere Troiae' — accusative and infinitive after 'fas': 'that the realms of Troy should rise again'. The plural 'regna' is poetic; Troy will rise again as Rome.

sentences.t: Durate, et vosmet rebus servate secundis.”
sentences.l: Endure, and yourselves for favourable circumstances preserve.”
sentences.i: Hold on, and keep yourselves safe for better days.”
sentences.n: 'durate' — imperative, 'harden yourselves, hold out'. 'vosmet' — 'you yourselves', 'vos' strengthened by the ending '-met'. 'rebus secundis' — 'for favourable circumstances' ('secundus' is literally 'following', hence 'favouring, fortunate'). The speech ends on the hope of better times.

sentences.t:
Talia voce refert, curisque ingentibus aeger
spem voltu simulat, premit altum corde dolorem.
sentences.l:
Such things in speech he returns, and with huge cares sick
hope in his face he feigns, he presses the deep grief in his heart.
sentences.i: So he speaks aloud; but sick with enormous cares he wears hope on his face and keeps the deep grief pressed down in his heart.
sentences.n: 'Talia voce refert' — 'refert' ('brings back') here simply means 'says, utters'. 'voce' — 'in speech, aloud', as opposed to what he feels. The line pair is built on a contrast: voice and face show hope, the heart ('corde') holds grief. 'aeger' — 'sick' with worry, nominative agreeing with 'he'. 'voltu' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultu' (face); you'll see 'volnus', 'divom', 'volgus' in the same style. The leader who hides his fear from his men is a figure Virgil returns to.

sentences.t: Illi se praedae accingunt, dapibusque futuris;
sentences.l: They themselves for the booty gird, and for feasts to come;
sentences.i: They gird themselves for the kill and for the feast to come;
sentences.n: 'Illi' — 'they', his men, the subject of the next five lines. 'se accingunt' — 'gird themselves', i.e. tuck up their clothes for work; 'praedae' and 'dapibus' are datives of purpose, 'for the booty, for the feasts'. 'futuris' — 'for the coming feasts'. The slaughter and cooking of the stags (see the end of aeneid-002) is a typical epic scene, with its fixed steps.

sentences.t: tergora deripiunt costis et viscera nudant;
sentences.l: hides they tear from ribs and entrails they lay bare;
sentences.i: they strip the hides from the ribs and lay the entrails bare;
sentences.n: 'tergora' — hides (an archaic word for skins); 'costis' — dative of separation, used in verse for 'from the ribs'. The sequence of these lines — flaying, cutting, skewering, boiling — is a stock epic feast, the kind Homer describes in great detail.

sentences.t: pars in frusta secant veribusque trementia figunt;
sentences.l: part into pieces cut and on spits the quivering fix;
sentences.i: some cut the meat in pieces and skewer the quivering flesh on spits;
sentences.n: 'pars… alii' (next line) — 'part… others': the division of labour. 'in frusta' — 'into pieces'. 'trementia' — 'the quivering (pieces)', neuter plural participle used as a noun: the meat is still twitching. 'veribus' — ablative, 'on spits'.

sentences.t: litore aena locant alii, flammasque ministrant.
sentences.l: on the shore bronze cauldrons set others, and flames supply.
sentences.i: others set bronze cauldrons along the shore and tend the fires.
sentences.n: 'aena' — 'bronze things', i.e. cauldrons (neuter plural adjective as a noun). 'litore' — ablative of place without a preposition, as often in verse. 'flammas ministrant' — 'supply the flames': 'ministrare' means to attend, serve, provide.

sentences.t:
Tum victu revocant vires, fusique per herbam
implentur veteris Bacchi pinguisque ferinae.
sentences.l:
Then with food they restore their strength, and stretched out over the grass
they are filled with old Bacchus and with fat game.
sentences.i: Then food calls their strength back; they sprawl in the grass and take their fill of aged wine and the rich meat of the hunt.
sentences.n: 'victu' — ablative of 'victus', 'food'. 'revocant vires' — 'call back strength', as with 'revocate animos' in the speech above. 'fusi' — 'poured out, stretched out', from 'fundo'. 'implentur… Bacchi… ferinae' — 'are filled of old Bacchus and fat game': the genitive follows verbs of filling. 'Bacchus' stands for wine, by metonymy: the god for what he gives. 'veteris' — the wine was given by Acestes in Sicily (see aeneid-002), which makes it old. 'ferina' — the flesh of wild animals (understand 'caro').

sentences.t:
Postquam exempta fames epulis mensaeque remotae,
amissos longo socios sermone requirunt,
spemque metumque inter dubii, seu vivere credant,
sive extrema pati nec iam exaudire vocatos.
sentences.l:
After hunger was removed by the feast and the tables cleared away,
the lost companions in long talk they ask after,
both hope and fear between wavering, whether to be living they should believe them,
or the last things to be suffering and no longer to hear when called.
sentences.i: When the feast had put hunger away and the tables were cleared, they talk long of the friends they have lost, hanging between hope and fear: are they to think them living, or to think they have suffered the end and can no longer hear when called?
sentences.n: 'Postquam exempta (est) fames epulis' — 'after hunger was removed by the feasting': the verb 'est' is left out. 'mensaeque remotae (sunt)' — the second clause also lacks its verb. 'requirunt' — 'ask after, seek'. 'inter' is placed after its nouns (anastrophe), 'spemque metumque inter': 'between hope and fear'. 'seu… credant, sive…' — 'whether they should believe': a subjunctive of deliberation in an indirect question. 'extrema pati' — 'to suffer the last things', i.e. to be dead. 'nec iam exaudire vocatos' — 'and no longer to hear when called': the ritual call to the dead, the 'conclamatio', at which the friends were last addressed.

sentences.t:
Praecipue pius Aeneas nunc acris Oronti,
nunc Amyci casum gemit et crudelia secum
fata Lyci, fortemque Gyan, fortemque Cloanthum.
sentences.l:
Above all pious Aeneas now of keen Orontes,
now of Amycus the fall laments, and the cruel with himself
fate of Lycus, and brave Gyas, and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.i: Above all, loyal Aeneas grieves — now for fierce Orontes' fall, now for Amycus's, and in silence for Lycus's cruel fate, and for brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.n: 'pius Aeneas' — the epithet that marks him: 'pius' is dutiful to gods, family and country (the noun 'pietas' was named in line 10 and again at 151; this is the adjective's first appearance). 'nunc… nunc' — 'now… now'. 'Oronti' is the genitive of the Greek name 'Orontes' (an -i genitive, like 'Achilli'); compare the Greek accusative 'Gyan' for Gyas. 'acris' — genitive singular of 'acer', 'keen, fierce'. 'casum gemit' — 'laments the fall of'. 'secum' — 'with himself', that is, silently, in his own mind. 'fata Lyci' — the 'fata' of a man are his lot or end, here his death. The roll-call of names is the same kind Virgil used in the storm; Orontes was last seen going down with his ship in the storm (I.113–117); the others are simply unaccounted for.

sentences.t:
Et iam finis erat, cum Iuppiter aethere summo
despiciens mare velivolum terrasque iacentis
litoraque et latos populos, sic vertice caeli
constitit, et Libyae defixit lumina regnis.
sentences.l:
And now an end there was, when Jupiter from highest aether
looking down on the sail-flying sea and lying lands
and shores and wide peoples, thus on the peak of heaven
stood, and on Libya's realms fixed his eyes.
sentences.i: And now it was ending, when Jupiter, looking down from highest heaven on the sea where sails go flying, the outspread lands, the coasts and the widespread peoples, halted on the peak of the sky and fixed his eyes on the kingdoms of Libya.
sentences.n: 'Et iam finis erat' — 'and now there was an end', of the meal and the talk; The action jumps to heaven, a fixed move in epic (compare the opening of the Odyssey, and Iliad 24). 'velivolum' — 'sail-flying', a compound in the manner of Greek epithets: the sea over which sails fly. 'iacentis' — 'lying (spread out)', agreeing with 'terras'; it is again the -is accusative plural. 'sic' — 'in this way', i.e. as he looked; 'vertice caeli' — on the 'peak, top' of heaven. 'defixit lumina' — 'fixed his eyes', 'lumina' being literally 'lights'. The view of the whole world is the place from which the prophecy that follows can be spoken.

sentences.t:
Atque illum talis iactantem pectore curas
tristior et lacrimis oculos suffusa nitentis
adloquitur Venus:
sentences.l:
And him, such cares tossing in his breast,
sadder, and with tears her shining eyes suffused,
addresses Venus:
sentences.i: As he turns such thoughts over in his heart, Venus, sadder than her wont, her shining eyes brimming with tears, speaks to him:
sentences.n: 'Atque illum… iactantem' — 'and him tossing', the object of 'adloquitur': 'illum' (Jupiter) is the one addressed. 'talis… curas' — 'such cares' are the cares he is turning over, which Venus is about to voice; the line leads straight into her speech. 'tristior' — comparative, 'sadder (than usual)'. 'oculos suffusa' — 'suffused as to her eyes': a participle with an accusative of the part affected, a construction taken from Greek (the 'Greek accusative'); 'nitentis' is again the -is accusative plural, 'shining'. The Venus of epic can be a petitioner as well as a goddess, and here her tears are meant to move the father of the gods.

sentences.t:
“O qui res hominumque deumque
aeternis regis imperiis, et fulmine terres,
quid meus Aeneas in te committere tantum,
quid Troes potuere, quibus, tot funera passis,
cunctus ob Italiam terrarum clauditur orbis?
sentences.l:
“O you who the affairs of men and of gods
with eternal commands rule, and with the thunderbolt terrify,
what so great against you to commit could my Aeneas,
what could the Trojans, to whom, so many deaths having suffered,
the whole circle of the lands is shut on account of Italy?
sentences.i: “Ruler of the affairs of gods and men by everlasting command, who strike terror with your thunderbolt, what wrong so grave could my Aeneas do you, what could the Trojans, who after so many deaths see the whole circle of the earth barred to them for Italy's sake?
sentences.n: Venus's complaint opens in the form of a prayer: 'O qui… regis' — the address of the god in his titles ('the one who rules'). 'res hominumque deumque' — the double '-que… -que' ('both… and', you'll see this constantly), with the genitives of 'homines' and 'dei' (the short form 'deum' of 'deorum'; compare 'divom'). 'imperiis' is ablative of means. 'quid… potuere' — 'what could they (do)': 'potuere' is 'potuerunt' (the '-ere' for '-erunt' again), and 'committere' is understood from the first question. 'quibus' — dative of disadvantage: the world 'is shut to them'. 'tot funera passis' — 'having suffered so many deaths'. 'cunctus ob Italiam… orbis' — the 'orbis terrarum', the circle of lands, closed against them; 'ob' means 'on account of, because of': the world is closed to them for Italy's sake.

sentences.t:
Certe hinc Romanos olim, volventibus annis,
hinc fore ductores, revocato a sanguine Teucri,
qui mare, qui terras omni dicione tenerent,
pollicitus, quae te, genitor, sententia vertit?
sentences.l:
Surely from here the Romans one day, as the years roll,
from here would be leaders, from the renewed blood of Teucer,
who sea, who lands with all dominion would hold,
you promised — what purpose, father, has turned you?
sentences.i: You promised, surely, that from this stock, in the rolling years, Roman leaders would one day rise, the blood of Teucer called back, to hold sea and land under their whole dominion — what thought has turned you, father?
sentences.n: A long sentence in which the main verb is held to the end: 'pollicitus' (the perfect participle of a deponent verb, 'having promised', with 'es' understood) governs an accusative and infinitive, 'Romanos… fore ductores' ('that the Romans would be leaders'; 'fore' = 'futuros esse'). 'certe' — 'surely, at any rate'. 'hinc… hinc' — 'from here (from Aeneas)'. 'volventibus annis' — 'with years rolling': the ablative absolute, a stock epic phrase for the passing of time. 'revocato a sanguine Teucri' — 'from the blood of Teucer called back': Teucer was the first king of Troy, from whom the Trojans are the 'Teucri'; the blood is 'renewed' in Rome. 'qui… tenerent' — relative clause of purpose or characteristic, subjunctive. 'omni dicione' — 'with all dominion, under complete rule'. 'quae te sententia vertit' — 'what judgement has turned you?' — which Jupiter will answer in 260.

sentences.t:
Hoc equidem occasum Troiae tristisque ruinas
solabar, fatis contraria fata rependens;
sentences.l:
With this indeed the fall of Troy and its sad ruins
I used to console, fates with contrary fates weighing against them;
sentences.i: It was this that eased my grief for Troy's fall and her sorrowful ruins: I would set fate against fate, the later against the earlier;
sentences.n: 'Hoc' — ablative, 'by this (promise)'. 'equidem' — 'for my part, indeed', emphatic first person. 'solabar' — imperfect, 'I used to console'. 'occasum Troiae' — 'the setting of Troy', as the sun sets: a metaphor for downfall. 'tristis ruinas' — the -is accusative plural again. 'fatis contraria fata rependens' — 'weighing contrary fates against fates': a balance, a bad fate set against a good one, the word 'fata' repeated for sharpness, in two cases next to each other.

sentences.t:
nunc eadem fortuna viros tot casibus actos
insequitur.
sentences.l:
now the same fortune men by so many misfortunes driven
pursues.
sentences.i: Now that same ill fortune hounds men already driven through so many disasters.
sentences.n: 'eadem fortuna' — 'the same fortune', the hostile fortune that destroyed Troy: it has not stopped. 'viros tot casibus actos' — 'men driven by so many misfortunes' (a perfect passive participle, 'actos', agrees with 'viros', the object of the verb in the next word). 'insequitur' — 'pursues', the sense 'harasses' coming from the hunt.

sentences.t: Quem das finem, rex magne, laborum?
sentences.l: What end do you give, great king, of toils?
sentences.i: What end do you grant to our labours, great king?
sentences.n: 'quem das finem… laborum' — 'what end do you give of the toils': the genitive of the thing ended. The question picks up Aeneas's own word, 'finem', from line 199 ('dabit deus his quoque finem'); Venus puts that hope to the god Aeneas was trusting. 'rex magne' — a king-title for Jupiter, who is at once king of the gods and the father.

sentences.t:
Antenor potuit, mediis elapsus Achivis,
Illyricos penetrare sinus, atque intima tutus
regna Liburnorum, et fontem superare Timavi,
unde per ora novem vasto cum murmure montis
it mare proruptum et pelago premit arva sonanti.
sentences.l:
Antenor was able, from the midst of the Achaeans having slipped away,
Illyrian gulfs to enter, and the inmost, safe,
realms of the Liburnians, and the spring to pass beyond of Timavus,
whence through nine mouths with vast roar of the mountain
goes the sea burst forth and with resounding flood presses the fields.
sentences.i: Antenor, slipping out from the midst of the Greeks, could thread the Illyrian gulfs and, safe, the inmost realms of the Liburnians, and pass beyond the spring of Timavus, where through nine mouths, with a vast roar from the mountain, the sea bursts forth and floods the fields with a booming tide.
sentences.n: Antenor, a Trojan elder who in Homer advised the Trojans to return Helen, was in later legend allowed to escape and settle in north-east Italy. 'mediis elapsus Achivis' — 'having slipped out from the midst of the Achaeans' (Greeks). 'potuit… penetrare… superare' — he 'could' enter and pass the Illyrian gulf (the head of the Adriatic), the 'intima regna' of the Liburnians (a people of the Dalmatian coast), and the spring of the Timavus (a river of the north Adriatic, with underground sources). 'tutus' — 'safe', agreeing with Antenor. The line 'it mare proruptum' — 'the sea goes burst forth' — describes the river as an arm of the sea breaking out through the cliff; 'ora novem' — 'nine mouths'. 'pelago… sonanti' — ablative of means, 'with a resounding flood'. A long geographical detour whose point is Venus's grievance: Antenor, a Trojan like Aeneas, did what Aeneas has not been allowed to do.

sentences.i: Yet there he founded the city of Patavium and a home for the Trojans, gave his people a name, and hung up the arms of Troy;
sentences.n: 'Hic tamen' — 'and yet here', in spite of his dangerous route. 'urbem Patavi' — Patavium (Padua). 'Teucrorum' — genitive plural, 'of the Teucrians' (Trojans), depending on 'sedes'; they are called 'Teucri' after their first king, Teucer. 'genti nomen dedit' — he gave his people a name; Virgil does not say which. 'arma fixit Troia' — he 'fixed up' Trojan arms: the dedication of weapons on a temple wall to mark the end of war. 'Troia' is an adjective, neuter plural, agreeing with 'arma'.

sentences.t: nunc placida compostus pace quiescit:
sentences.l: now in peaceful calm laid to rest he reposes:
sentences.i: and now, laid to rest in untroubled peace, he sleeps:
sentences.n: 'compostus' — Greenough's spelling of the perfect participle of 'compono', 'laid to rest, composed', a contracted form of 'compositus' that the verse also uses elsewhere; the word often means 'laid in the tomb'. 'placida pace' — 'in peaceful peace', with the adjective added for emphasis. 'quiescit' — 'rests', a verb for sleep and for death.

sentences.t:
nos, tua progenies, caeli quibus adnuis arcem,
navibus (infandum!) amissis, unius ob iram
prodimur atque Italis longe disiungimur oris.
sentences.l:
we, your offspring, to whom you nod heaven's citadel,
ships (unspeakable!) lost, on account of one's anger
are betrayed and from the Italian shores far are parted.
sentences.i: We, your own blood, to whom you grant the citadel of heaven with a nod, have lost our ships — a thing beyond speech — and, for one goddess's anger, are handed over and held far from the shores of Italy.
sentences.n: 'nos, tua progenies' — 'we, your offspring': the Trojans descend from Jupiter through his son Dardanus, and Aeneas is his grandson through Venus, the god's daughter. 'quibus caeli arcem adnuis' — 'to whom you nod the citadel of heaven', i.e. you grant by nodding assent, the god's gesture; the 'arx' is heaven itself, the place among the gods that Jupiter has promised Aeneas (see his answer at 259–260). The parenthesis '(infandum!)' — 'unspeakable thing!' — is a cry from the heart. 'unius ob iram' — 'on account of the anger of one (Juno)'. 'prodimur' — 'we are handed over, betrayed'. 'Italis… oris' — 'Italian shores', ablative of separation. Venus never names Juno: she is 'one' whose anger is enough.

sentences.t: Hic pietatis honos?
sentences.l: This the honour of piety?
sentences.i: Is this the honour paid to piety?
sentences.n: 'Hic pietatis honos?' — an exclamation with no verb, 'Is this the honour of piety?' The question is not a request for an answer. 'pietas' is the central virtue of the poem: dutiful loyalty to gods, kin and country, the quality that gives Aeneas his epithet. Venus's argument is that he has been loyal, and fortune has not rewarded it.

sentences.t: Sic nos in sceptra reponis?”
sentences.l: Thus us to sceptres do you restore?”
sentences.i: Is this how you set us back on the throne?”
sentences.n: 'reponis' — 'put back, restore': the word suggests a kingdom Aeneas is owed (his claim to Troy's throne). 'sceptra' — 'sceptres', for kingly power, in the plural. 'in sceptra' — 'to power'. Her speech ends where it began, on the issue of what Jupiter has promised and what he has done.

sentences.t:
Olli subridens hominum sator atque deorum,
voltu, quo caelum tempestatesque serenat,
oscula libavit natae, dehinc talia fatur:
sentences.l:
To her smiling, the begetter of men and of gods,
with that look with which sky and storms he clears,
kisses he touched on his daughter, then such things says:
sentences.i: Smiling at her, the sire of men and gods, with the countenance that brightens the sky and stills its storms, touched his daughter's lips with a kiss, and then spoke:
sentences.n: 'Olli' — an old form of 'illi', 'to her'; Virgil uses it for a solemn tone. 'hominum sator atque deorum' — 'begetter of men and gods', 'sator' being the one who sows, a father in the widest sense; 'deorum' is the ordinary genitive plural beside the older 'divom' (and 'hominum'). 'voltu, quo caelum tempestatesque serenat' — 'with the face with which he clears the sky and the storms': it recalls Neptune's calming of the sea in the previous part. 'oscula libavit' — 'he touched (sipped) kisses', lightly. 'natae' — dative of the person kissed. 'talia fatur' — 'says such things', the formula that introduces a speech.

sentences.t: “Parce metu, Cytherea:
sentences.l: “Refrain from fear, Cytherea:
sentences.i: “Lay your fear aside, Cytherea:
sentences.n: 'Parce metu' — 'spare (yourself) fear': 'parco' with the ablative or dative means 'refrain from'. 'Cytherea' — Venus, named for the island of Cythera, where she came ashore from the sea. Jupiter's answer begins with a reassurance, and the whole speech answers Venus point by point.

sentences.t:
manent immota tuorum
fata tibi;
sentences.l:
remain unmoved of your own
the fates for you;
sentences.i: your people's fates stand fixed and unmoved for you;
sentences.n: 'manent immota… fata' — 'remain unmoved, the fates': 'immota' is a neuter plural adjective with 'fata'. 'tuorum' — 'of your own (people)', the genitive plural of 'tuus', used as a noun. 'tibi' — dative, 'for you'. This is the answer to Venus's question about 'fata contraria': nothing has changed.

sentences.i: you will behold the city, the promised walls of Lavinium, and carry high-hearted Aeneas up, aloft, to the stars of heaven;
sentences.n: 'promissa Lavini moenia' — 'the promised walls of Lavinium' (the town Aeneas will found in Latium and name for Lavinia, his future wife, though she has not yet been mentioned): the genitive 'Lavini' is placed in the middle to frame 'promissa… moenia'. 'sublimem' — 'lifted high', a predicate adjective. 'ad sidera' — 'to the stars', the gods' place: Aeneas will be made a god. 'magnanimum' — accusative singular, agreeing with 'Aenean': 'great-souled Aeneas'. 'Aenean' — Greek accusative.

sentences.t: neque me sententia vertit.
sentences.l: nor me has any purpose turned.
sentences.i: and no change of mind has turned me.
sentences.n: 'neque me sententia vertit' — 'nor has any purpose turned me': a direct answer to Venus's 'quae te… sententia vertit?' in line 237, reusing her verb and her noun. 'sententia' — a decision, a view; Venus asked what new decision had turned him from his promise, and he says none has.

sentences.t:
Hic tibi (fabor enim, quando haec te cura remordet,
longius et volvens fatorum arcana movebo)
bellum ingens geret Italia, populosque feroces
contundet, moresque viris et moenia ponet,
sentences.l:
This man for you (I shall speak, for, since this care gnaws you back,
further, and unrolling the secrets of the fates, I shall stir them)
a great war will wage in Italy, and fierce peoples
will crush, and customs for the men and walls will set,
sentences.i: He — for I will tell you, since this worry keeps biting at you, and I shall unroll the hidden records of the fates and bring them out at fuller length — will fight a great war for you in Italy, break fierce peoples, and set up customs and walls for his men,
sentences.n: 'Hic' — 'this man' (Aeneas), the subject of the three verbs 'geret', 'contundet', 'ponet'; it is held back across a long parenthesis. The parenthesis explains why Jupiter will say more than she asked: 'fabor enim' ('I shall speak, for'), 'quando' ('since'), 'haec te cura remordet' ('this care gnaws you again', 're-' marking the repeated bite). 'longius' — 'further than before'. 'volvens' — 'unrolling', the image of a scroll, a record of destiny (the 'fatorum arcana', secret things of the fates). 'movebo' — 'I shall stir, reveal'. 'tibi' — dative of interest, 'for you'. 'bellum… geret' — 'will wage a war' (the war of Books 7–12). 'moresque viris et moenia ponet' — 'will set up customs and walls for his men': he will give laws and a city to a people not yet settled.

sentences.t:
tertia dum Latio regnantem viderit aestas,
ternaque transierint Rutulis hiberna subactis.
sentences.l:
until the third summer has seen him reigning in Latium,
and three winters have passed, the Rutulians having been subdued.
sentences.i: until the third summer has seen him reigning in Latium, and three winters have gone by with the Rutulians conquered.
sentences.n: 'dum… viderit' — 'until the third summer shall have seen him': 'dum' meaning 'until' takes a perfect subjunctive of expectation (its form coincides with the future perfect), looking forward to a time-limit; 'transierint' in the next line is the same. 'regnantem' — 'him reigning'. The time-count is three summers and three winters — three years of kingship in Latium. 'Rutulis subactis' — ablative absolute, 'the Rutulians having been subdued': the people of Turnus, Aeneas's enemy in the second half of the poem.

sentences.t:
At puer Ascanius, cui nunc cognomen Iulo
additur,—Ilus erat, dum res stetit Ilia regno,—
triginta magnos volvendis mensibus orbis
imperio explebit, regnumque ab sede Lavini
transferet, et longam multa vi muniet Albam.
sentences.l:
But the boy Ascanius, to whom now the surname Iulus
is added,—Ilus he was, while the Ilian state stood in kingship,—
thirty great circles with rolling months
in rule he will fill, and the kingdom from the seat of Lavinium
will transfer, and long Alba with much strength fortify.
sentences.i: But the boy Ascanius, who is now given the added name Iulus — he was Ilus while the Ilian state stood as a kingdom — will reign through thirty full years, each a great circle of turning months, move his kingdom from its seat at Lavinium, and fortify Long Alba with mighty strength.
sentences.n: 'At puer Ascanius' — Aeneas's son, who becomes a second founder. 'cui nunc cognomen Iulo additur' — 'to whom the surname Iulus is now added': the dative 'Iulo' is the name in agreement with 'cui' (a dative of the name, like 'nomen est mihi'). The aside between the dashes is the play on names: 'Ilus' (his Trojan name, from Ilium) turns into 'Iulus', from which the gens Iulia, Caesar's family, claims descent. 'triginta magnos volvendis mensibus orbis' — 'thirty great circles', i.e. years, 'with months to be rolled' (a gerundive, 'volvendis'): the year as the circle of its months. 'imperio explebit' — 'will fill out with his rule'. 'longam Albam' — Alba Longa, 'Long Alba', the city that will precede Rome.

sentences.t:
Hic iam ter centum totos regnabitur annos
gente sub Hectorea, donec regina sacerdos,
Marte gravis, geminam partu dabit Ilia prolem.
sentences.l:
Here now three hundred whole years it will be reigned
under the Hectorean race, until a priestess queen,
heavy with Mars, twin offspring in birth will give, Ilia.
sentences.i: Here, for three hundred full years, the kingship will rest with Hector's line, until a priestess-queen, Ilia, heavy with Mars's child, bears twin sons.
sentences.n: 'regnabitur' — an impersonal passive: 'it will be reigned', i.e. there will be kingship (you'll see this constantly with intransitive verbs). 'ter centum totos annos' — 'for three hundred entire years'. 'gente sub Hectorea' — 'under the Hectorean race': the line of Aeneas is called Hector's, since the Trojans are the people of Hector. 'regina sacerdos' — Ilia (also Rhea Silvia), a Vestal and royal daughter. 'Marte gravis' — 'heavy with Mars', i.e. pregnant by the god of war. 'geminam partu dabit prolem' — 'will give twin offspring at one birth': Romulus and Remus.

sentences.t:
Inde lupae fulvo nutricis tegmine laetus
Romulus excipiet gentem, et Mavortia condet
moenia, Romanosque suo de nomine dicet.
sentences.l:
Then in the tawny cover of the wolf his nurse rejoicing
Romulus will take up the race, and Mavortian
walls will found, and Romans from his own name will call.
sentences.i: Then Romulus, proud in the tawny hide of the she-wolf who nursed him, will take up the leadership of the people, found the walls of Mars, and call them Romans after his own name.
sentences.n: 'lupae… nutricis tegmine' — 'in the covering of the nurse she-wolf': Romulus is pictured clad in the tawny hide of the wolf who suckled him. 'excipiet gentem' — 'will take up the people', as an heir takes up the leadership. 'Mavortia' — 'of Mavors', an old form of 'Mars'; Mars is Romulus's father. 'Romanosque suo de nomine dicet' — 'will call them Romans from his own name': 'Roma' and 'Romulus' share a root, a derivation accepted in antiquity.

sentences.t: His ego nec metas rerum nec tempora pono;
sentences.l: To these I neither bounds of things nor times set;
sentences.i: For them I set no limits of power and no span of time;
sentences.n: 'His' — dative, 'for these (Romans)'. 'metas rerum nec tempora' — 'neither bounds of power nor times': a 'meta' is a turning-post in a racecourse, hence a limit. The central claim of Jupiter's speech: there will be neither a spatial nor a temporal limit to Rome.

sentences.t: imperium sine fine dedi.
sentences.l: rule without end I have given.
sentences.i: I have granted them rule that knows no end.
sentences.n: 'imperium sine fine dedi' — 'I have given rule without end'. The perfect tense is a statement of a settled decision: the thing is as good as done. This is one of the best-known lines of the speech, and the 'imperium' promised is often called 'imperium sine fine', the ideology of Augustan Rome.

sentences.t:
Quin aspera Iuno,
quae mare nunc terrasque metu caelumque fatigat,
consilia in melius referet, mecumque fovebit
Romanos rerum dominos gentemque togatam:
sentences.l:
Nay more, harsh Juno,
who now sea and lands and sky with fear wearies,
her counsels to the better will bring back, and with me will cherish
the Romans, lords of affairs, and the toga-clad race:
sentences.i: Why, even harsh Juno, who now wears out sea and land and sky with terror, will turn her purposes to kinder ones, and join me in cherishing the Romans, masters of the world, the people of the toga:
sentences.n: 'Quin' — 'nay more, indeed', adding a further point. 'aspera Iuno' — Juno is 'harsh'; the poem has called her 'saeva', fierce, since its fourth line. 'metu… fatigat' — 'wearies with fear': she is the one frightening sea, land and sky. 'consilia in melius referet' — 'will bring her plans back to something better'. 'mecumque fovebit' — 'and will cherish with me'. 'rerum dominos' — 'lords of affairs', i.e. rulers of the world. 'gentem togatam' — 'the toga-wearing people': the toga is the Roman civilian dress, a mark of peace and citizenship.

sentences.t: sic placitum.
sentences.l: so it has been decided.
sentences.i: So it has been resolved.
sentences.n: 'sic placitum (est)' — 'thus it has pleased', 'thus it is decided': 'placitum' is the participle of 'placeo', used impersonally, with 'est' left out. The phrase marks a decree of Jupiter, which is also the voice of fate.

sentences.t:
Veniet lustris labentibus aetas,
cum domus Assaraci Phthiam clarasque Mycenas
servitio premet, ac victis dominabitur Argis.
sentences.l:
There will come, as the lustra slip by, an age,
when the house of Assaracus Phthia and famed Mycenae
with servitude will press, and over conquered Argos will rule.
sentences.i: In time, as the lustra slip away, an age will come when the house of Assaracus will weigh Phthia and renowned Mycenae down with slavery and hold sway over vanquished Argos.
sentences.n: 'lustris labentibus' — 'with lustra gliding by' (ablative absolute): a 'lustrum' is a five-year period, the interval at which Romans took the census and purified the city. 'domus Assaraci' — the house of Assaracus, a Trojan king, ancestor of Aeneas, so the Trojans' descendants, the Romans. 'Phthiam clarasque Mycenas' — Phthia was Achilles' home, Mycenae Agamemnon's: the homelands of Troy's destroyers. 'servitio premet' — 'will press with slavery'. 'victis dominabitur Argis' — 'will rule over conquered Argos' (dative with 'dominor'); Rome's conquest of Greece in the second century BC, set as the reversal of the Trojan War.

sentences.t:
Nascetur pulchra Troianus origine Caesar,
imperium oceano, famam qui terminet astris,—
Iulius, a magno demissum nomen Iulo.
sentences.l:
There will be born, of fair origin, a Trojan Caesar,
who shall bound his empire with Ocean, his fame with the stars,—
Julius, a name handed down from great Iulus.
sentences.i: From a splendid line a Trojan Caesar shall be born, one who will bound his empire with Ocean and his fame with the stars — Julius, a name drawn down from great Iulus.
sentences.n: 'Troianus Caesar' — the Caesar of the line of Troy; which Caesar is left open, and the identity (Augustus, whom Virgil's first readers took it to be, or Julius Caesar) has been disputed since. 'qui terminet' — 'who shall bound': the relative clause with the subjunctive gives purpose or character. 'imperium oceano, famam astris' — a pair of boundaries, empire's limit at Ocean (the stream encircling the world), fame's at the stars; compare 'ad sidera' in 259. 'Iulius… demissum nomen Iulo' — 'Julius, a name sent down from great Iulus', the connection of the Julian family with Ascanius.

sentences.t:
Hunc tu olim caelo, spoliis Orientis onustum,
accipies secura;
sentences.l:
Him you one day in heaven, with the spoils of the East laden,
will receive, free of care;
sentences.i: You, no longer afraid, will one day welcome him into heaven, laden with the spoils of the East;
sentences.n: 'Hunc' — 'this man' (the Caesar), emphatic first word. 'olim' — 'some day', looking far ahead. 'spoliis Orientis onustum' — 'laden with the spoils of the East' (a reference to the victories in Asia and Egypt). 'secura' — 'free from care', agreeing with 'tu' (Venus). The Caesar is to be received into heaven, an apotheosis, like Aeneas.

sentences.t: vocabitur hic quoque votis.
sentences.l: he will be called upon in vows also, this one.
sentences.i: he too will be invoked in prayers.
sentences.n: 'vocabitur… votis' — 'will be called by vows', i.e. he will receive prayers (and so will be a god). 'hic quoque' — 'this one too', as Aeneas is to join the gods.

sentences.t: Aspera tum positis mitescent saecula bellis;
sentences.l: Harsh then, wars having been laid aside, will grow mild the ages;
sentences.i: Then wars will be laid aside, and the harsh ages will grow gentle;
sentences.n: 'Aspera… saecula' — 'the harsh ages' (the age that was hard with war), the subject of 'mitescent'. 'positis bellis' — 'wars having been put down', ablative absolute. The word order puts 'aspera' first and 'bellis' last to frame the line. The Augustan peace is presented as the end of ages of fighting.

sentences.t:
cana Fides, et Vesta, Remo cum fratre Quirinus,
iura dabunt;
sentences.l:
grey Faith, and Vesta, with brother Remus Quirinus,
laws will give;
sentences.i: white-haired Faith and Vesta, and Quirinus with his brother Remus, will give the law;
sentences.n: 'cana Fides' — 'hoary Faith', Good Faith as a personified goddess, grey-haired as the ancient emblem of trust. 'Vesta' — goddess of the hearth. 'Remo cum fratre Quirinus' — 'Quirinus with his brother Remus': Quirinus is the deified Romulus; the brothers are reconciled after the old fratricide. 'iura dabunt' — 'will give laws', the subject being all of those named.

sentences.t:
dirae ferro et compagibus artis
claudentur Belli portae;
sentences.l:
dread with iron and with tight bonds
will be closed the gates of War;
sentences.i: the dread gates of War will be shut with iron and tight-fastened joints;
sentences.n: 'dirae… Belli portae' — 'the dread gates of War', framing the clause; 'Bellum' is personified. The Romans kept the gates of the temple of Janus open in wartime and shut them in peace; Augustus shut them in 29 BC. 'ferro et compagibus artis' — 'with iron and tight joints'. 'claudentur' — passive future.

sentences.t:
Furor impius intus,
saeva sedens super arma, et centum vinctus aenis
post tergum nodis, fremet horridus ore cruento.”
sentences.l:
Impious Frenzy within,
sitting on savage arms, and, bound with a hundred bronze
knots behind the back, will roar, bristling, with bloody mouth.”
sentences.i: and inside, impious Frenzy, sitting on a pile of fierce weapons, bound behind the back with a hundred bronze knots, will roar, bristling, his mouth red with blood.”
sentences.n: 'Furor impius' — Frenzy (the madness of war) as a personified figure, shut up inside the temple. 'saeva sedens super arma' — 'sitting on savage arms', a sound-pattern with 's'. 'centum vinctus aenis post tergum nodis' — 'bound with a hundred bronze knots behind the back', the adjective 'aenis' and noun 'nodis' enclosing 'post tergum'. 'fremet horridus ore cruento' — 'will roar, bristling, with bloody mouth'. The closing quotation mark ends Jupiter's speech, one of the poem's fullest statements of Rome's destiny: war overcome and bound by Roman peace.
